reading.body:
Gregory Meeks took $21,500 in AI-company PAC money across 2025 and 2026 while sponsoring and cosponsoring AI export-control bills and voting yes on every AI bill recorded here.

The pattern is a single member whose AI record runs on two tracks at once. The money is steady and small: eleven contributions from Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic committees, ranging from $1,000 to $3,000, spread across fourteen months. The legislation is narrower and more specific. He sponsored the RESTRICT Act, which addresses export and security trade restrictions for integrated circuit technologies, and cosponsored the AI OVERWATCH Act on oversight of verified exports and restrictions on weaponizable advanced technology. Both are export-control bills, which is the part of AI policy that touches chips directly.

That matters because compute is the constraint, and export controls are the mechanism by which the United States tries to hold it. A member who writes chip-export restrictions and takes money from the companies most affected by them is the ordinary shape of American technology policy, not an anomaly. The contributions are disclosed, dated, and traceable to filings, which is what makes the pairing legible at all.

What the data does not show is causation, and it does not try to. The dates are placed in order so they can be read together, not to claim one produced the other. The four recorded votes are on bills identified only by number, so the data does not say what H.R. 7757, H.R. 5764, H.R. 1770, or S. 146 contain or whether they concern AI at all. The contribution totals cover only committees that filed, only the amounts listed, and only this member's receipts, not spending. Nothing here covers data centers, power procurement, or the grid, so no claim about the physical buildout can be drawn from it.
